**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

Words are like feathers—light, drifting, capable of lifting or suffocating. A thousand of them could fill a book, a speech, a lifetime of unsent letters. Or they could be a single breath held too long, a sigh that never escapes.

I think about the first word I ever spoke. Was it "mama"? "Papa"? Or something meaningless, a sound before meaning, like the hum of a refrigerator in an empty room? Words are how we stitch ourselves to the world, how we name the unnamed. Without them, we are just bodies in space, breathing, but not *saying*. Not *being heard*.

And yet—what if words are also cages? Every label we give a thing, every definition, every story we tell to make sense of the chaos—aren’t they just prisons of our own making? Love is a word, but love is also the ache in your chest when you think of someone who doesn’t think of you. Freedom is a word, but freedom is also the weight of choices you never wanted to make. God, death, justice, hope—words that shape civilizations, that start wars, that end them. Words that can heal or destroy with the same breath.

I wonder if the people who came before us had the same struggle. Did they wake up and think, *Today, I will write my name into the world*? Or did they just live, day by day, until the words came later, when the silence grew too loud? History is just a collection of words, after all. The winners write it. The losers are erased. But the erasure is a word too—*forgotten*, *lost*, *never existed*. Even absence is a kind of language.

What if I told you that every word I write now is a lie? Not in the sense that it’s false, but in the sense that language itself is a lie. It promises precision, but all it offers is approximation. You say "tree," and I picture an oak, but you picture a willow. You say "sad," and I feel a hollow in my ribs, but you feel a weight on your shoulders. Words are bridges made of smoke. They connect us, but they can also burn.

And yet—we can’t stop using them. Even this, right now, is a surrender to the need to be understood. To be *seen*. To take the chaos inside and shape it into something another person can hold, even for a moment. That’s the magic of it, isn’t it? The alchemy of turning breath into meaning.

But what if the meaning is the problem? What if the thousand words I write today are just echoes of a thousand words I’ve read, a thousand voices that shaped me before I even knew I was being shaped? What if I’m not the author of this, but just a scribe for something older, something deeper?

I think about the last word I’ll ever say. Will it be a name? A plea? A curse? Or will I just stop, mid-sentence, and the world will keep turning, indifferent, because words are temporary, but the silence they leave behind is eternal.

Or maybe the last word doesn’t matter. Maybe the last word is the one that was never spoken. The one that lived in the throat, heavy as a stone, until the throat opened and let it out—or didn’t.

I could write a thousand words about silence. About how it’s not the absence of sound, but the presence of everything else. The hum of the universe. The pulse of blood in your ears. The whisper of time passing. Silence is where words go to die, but also where they are born.

So here I am, writing. Filling the page with ink that will fade, with sentences that will crumble into dust. And yet—here we are, you and I, connected by these fragile marks on a screen. You’re reading this, aren’t you? That means something. It means the words did their job, even if only for a moment.

Maybe that’s all we ever do. Write our thousand words into the void, hoping someone, somewhere, will pause and listen. Not because the words are perfect, but because they’re *ours*. Because they’re the closest thing we have to touching another soul.

So take this. Take these thousand words. And if you remember one, if one line lingers in your mind like a half-remembered dream, then I’ve done my part. The rest is yours.
